Christa Pike 'angry and confused' about Tennessee's failed execution effort, lawyers say

Her lawyers said she has pneumonia, severe swelling and difficulty eating and moving her arms, while Tennessee has suspended executions for the rest of the year.

WASHINGTON: Christa Pike , sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke "angry and confused" in a hospital this week with a long recuperation ahead after surviving Tennessee's botched effort to execute her, her lawyers said on Wednesday (Oct 7). A week ago, Pike , 50, was taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections of the caustic barbiturate pentobarbital failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. As late as Monday, her lawyers believed Pike was brain dead and that life support would be removed the next day following the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, which has renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US. "But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team, and including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking," Randall Spivey, one of her lawyers, told reporters after a court hearing on Wednesday, where a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve syringes and other evidence from the botched execution.

"She is angry and confused about everything right now," Spivey said. "She is very aware that the state tried to execute her." Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look into the botched executions of Pike and of Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines. Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, facing a long road to recovery, her lawyers said. She cannot swallow or eat, has pneumonia, cannot move her "tremendously swollen" hands or arms, and it is unclear if she will regain her lost mobility, they said. Although she still has "cognitive confusion," the lawyers said, she has been speaking with those around her. "She has wanted to know what's happened, and she's asked about several people," Spivey said. "She's asked about the victim's family." Pike was sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the 1995 torture and murder of her 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer. She is the first person known to have survived a "completed execution attempt" in the US, her lawyers say, calling it a violation of the Constitution's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishments.

A UNIQUE CASE Pike 's lawyers are unexpectedly continuing their litigation against state officials, seeking to pierce the secrecy that normally surrounds execution procedures in Tennessee and other states. Earlier on Wednesday, a judge in Davidson County Chancery Court, I'Ashea Myles, agreed to order Tennessee officials to preserve all evidence from the failed execution, including syringes, drug packaging and lot numbers, catheters, intravenous lines and gurney restraints. The all-female execution team requested by Pike used at least seven needles during a grueling ordeal that lasted more than two hours, and one needle was bent 90 degrees when it was pulled out, her lawyers said. Myles largely sided with Pike 's lawyers at the end of Wednesday's hearing, describing the litigation, which began in January in an effort to prevent the scheduled execution, as unusual because no one had anticipated Pike surviving. "This case is unique, to say the least," Myles said. She also ordered the state to preserve internal communications about the attempted execution, including incident reports, witness accounts and encrypted messages. She has yet to rule on a request by Pike 's lawyers that the Tennessee Department of Correction let them take any residual traces of the execution drugs for chemical analysis. The Tennessee Department of Correction has opposed what it says is a "duplicative and unnecessary" preservation order, arguing it is already legally required to preserve all evidence and that it was already willing to share most, if not all, of what Pike 's lawyers sought.

Related:

Tennessee prison chief resigns after failed execution

Christa Pike gets 'life-saving medical care' after surviving Tennessee execution

Tennessee and other US states have long struggled to acquire execution drugs. They cannot be obtained from major pharmaceutical companies because of a European trade ban on companies that sell products for use in torture or executions. Tennessee, like other states, has turned to small, largely unregulated compounding pharmacies to make small batches of the drugs, promising to hide their identity. "Today's hearing was about transparency, about why Christa , the courts, the media and the public should not simply take the state's word about what happened last Wednesday," Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike , told reporters after the judge's ruling. He repeated the demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike 's sentence to life in prison and never attempt to execute her again. A spokesperson for Lee, who denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Pike 's lawyers had sought an alternative to lethal injections, saying her small veins and related medical conditions made her afraid that something would go wrong.

Source: Reuters/fs

Belgian students rally over education costs in protests echoing France

Local media reported that 107 people were arrested in Belgium in recent days.

High school students hold placards and shout slogans as they take part in a spontaneous street protest against education reforms introduced by the Wallonia-Brussels Federation government and an increase in student fees, in Liege, Belgium, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Stephanie Lecocq

LIEGE: Hundreds of students , inspired in part by education al unrest in neighbouring France , have taken to the streets of the Belgian city of Liège, with local media reporting 107 arrests in recent days. Local authorities could not immediately be reached to confirm the arrests, which the Belga news agency reported were linked to offences including property damage and arson. Students have protested over Belgium's French-language education system, citing rising education costs , over crowded classrooms and difficulties accessing study materials. They held signs with slogans including "It's a mess, we are fighting for a right! Not a privilege!" and "I chose education , not the hunger games!!".

The unrest follows June clashes between protesters and police in Brussels over education reforms, including a tuition increase for most students in Belgium's French-speaking Community to €1,194 (US$1,280) from €835. Videos circulating on social media in recent days showed shattered glass, fires and hundreds of mostly young protesters in Liège, while other footage showed police blocking roads. During Wednesday's protest, police were seen checking students for weapons.

A person throws an object into a burning structure on a street, on the day of a spontaneous street protest of high school students against education reforms introduced by the Wallonia-Brussels Federation government and an increase in student fees, in Liege, Belgium, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Stephanie Lecocq

IN TOUCH WITH FRENCH STUDENTS Some students told Reuters they were in touch with French counterparts. "We support each other because we're facing pretty much the same issues," 19-year-old student Alfred said. Amelia Di Salve, also 19, who is studying to become a teacher, said Belgium's student movement began earlier this year and was reignited after students saw the demonstrations in France . "When we saw nothing was changing without protests , we decided we would start ... France did influence us a little," she said. Liège mayor Willy Demeyer told Belgian broadcaster RTBF he hoped calm would return and "that dialogue can be established and that the young people can express their grievances in a peaceful way and, if possible, have those concerns heard".

US forces face curfew, alcohol ban in Japan's Okinawa after murder case

The presence of US forces has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents in Okinawa over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of its troops.

Demonstrators take part in a protest outside the Prime Minister's office following the killing of a Japanese woman in Okinawa, for which a US Marine is a suspect, in Tokyo, Japan, on Oct 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Kim Kyung-Hoon)

TOKYO: US soldiers stationed on Japan's Okinawa have been given a month-long curfew and banned from drinking alcohol while they undergo discipline training after a Marine was alleged to have murdered and robbed a local woman . Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southernmost prefecture, on Saturday (Oct 3) and taking her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said. The case is the latest in a string of incidents stretching back years that have fuelled unease over the large US troop presence on the island chain near Taiwan and China, with US officials warning it could undermine ties vital to security in East Asia. "Every interaction with our neighbours either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region," Lt Gen Benjamin Watson said in a statement on Tuesday ordering the measures.

All US military operations on Okinawa will be paused for 48 hours while troops undergo training on standards and discipline, Watson added. "BRUTAL AND HEINOUS" Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called Saturday's killing "extremely brutal and heinous". She said she had strongly protested to the United States and demanded measures to prevent such incidents in the future. Yagi died of asphyxiation after Ballard allegedly "pressed on her neck," police told the Stars and Stripes newspaper.

Devin Jacob Ballard, a U.S. Marine who has been in custody in an alleged robbery and murder of a woman on Japan's southern island of Okinawa, is sent over to the Naha prosecutors' office in Japan, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. (Kotaro Ueda/Kyodo News via AP)

Hotel staff found the woman unconscious in her room in the early hours of Saturday after she failed to check out. About 200 officers were involved in a search for the man earlier caught on CCTV entering the hotel with the victim, local media reported.  Okinawa Governor Genta Koja will meet Takaichi on Wednesday to discuss the response to the crime, which sparked protests in Naha and Tokyo. Japan hosts the largest overseas contingent of US forces globally. Most of the 18,000 Japan-based Marines are stationed in Okinawa, which the US held from the end of World War II until 1972. That presence has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of its troops. The 1995 rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three US servicemen sparked mass demonstrations. Saturday's killing could complicate Takaichi's efforts to relocate some Marines from the busy Futenma air base to a more remote facility at Henoko. Opponents want the troops moved out of the prefecture. Okinawa, which is 100km from Taiwan at the closest point, is viewed by Tokyo and Washington as key in deterring potential military aggression from China.

Source: Reuters/lk

Californians blast Trump remark that Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles, San Diego

California Governor Gavin Newsom denounced the Republican Trump as "deranged and dangerous".

LOS ANGELES: President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that Iran could "take out" a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego , drawing a swift rebuke from California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans. Trump, speaking at a political rally in the state's farm belt on Monday (Oct 5), discussed American wartime economic sacrifices and said he was determined to "see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did." "And again, remember, with the war, it's just artificial, it's a little bit high, it's a small price to pay," he told the crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, apparently referring to rising prices of fuel, fertiliser and other products attributed to energy market disruptions from the war. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it's going to be over with very soon," he said.

"It's essentially almost over with," Trump went on. "But it's going to end very soon, and it's going to end one way or the other." On Tuesday, the White House dismissed criticism of the remark. "The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung said in a social media post.  "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money." Trump has shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before, and he previously downplayed his concerns about the potential for Iran or its allies to launch an attack on US soil. EARLY VOTING UNDERWAY IN CALIFORNIA The comment in rural Nebraska, a state Trump won with more than 55 per cent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election, targeted Democratic-run cities in California, a solidly Democratic state the president often criticises. Monday's comments prompted a backlash from California officials. California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, denounced the Republican president as "deranged and dangerous". "After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego," he wrote on X. Newsom, who has positioned himself as a major political foil to Trump and is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, juxtaposed a video clip of Trump in Nebraska with mention of the president's previous rhetoric to justify deploying US military troops to Los Angeles and other cities to fight crime and enforce immigration.

Related:

Commentary: Why a booming economy is not helping Trump

Commentary: Who in Iran can make a deal with the US – and make it stick?

California's early voting for the November midterm elections started on Monday. The president's Republican Party has hoped to win more races in the state in recent years, including this year's gubernatorial election. Newsom championed the redrawing of California's congressional map last year to favour Democrats in this year's election after Trump pushed for conservative-led Texas to redraw its map to boost Republicans. One of the Republicans running in a competitive race in a redrawn California district near San Diego, Jim Desmond, distanced himself from Trump's remarks. "I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland," he wrote on X.  "No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage." US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in a competitive race in northern California, said in a statement that Trump's comment was "unhelpful". Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, said in a statement that Trump's comment "could potentially compromise our safety". Appearing on MS Now on Tuesday, Bass disputed Cheung's assertion that Trump's comments were being misinterpreted by a "freaked out" media. "Well, I'm not sure that he understands that we can hear what the president said," Bass countered, adding that Cheung's defence of Trump's remarks "has no connection to the words that came out of the president's mouth". Los Angeles and San Diego rank as the largest and second-largest cities in California by population. More than 115,000 active-duty service members are also stationed in San Diego, including Naval Base San Diego, the largest on the US West Coast. "My constituents - including many active duty service members, veterans, and their families - are not acceptable collateral damage in Trump’s stupid war," US Representative Sara Jacobs, a Democrat, said in a social media post.

In interview, US Vice President Vance says Iran must cut enrichment to end war

Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future drawdowns.

US Vice President JD Vance is interviewed by Reuters reporter Jacob Bogage before a campaign rally at Fairbanks International Airport in Fairbanks, Alaska, on Oct 5, 2026. (Photo: Jacquelyn Martin/Pool via REUTERS)

FAIRBANKS: US Vice President JD Vance said in an exclusive interview with Reuters that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations. Vance, a longtime sceptic of US involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in September that quickly fell apart. The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.  Speaking on Monday after a campaign trip in Alaska, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns. "If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 per cent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity." Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz , a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer and has warned that military operations could intensify after the midterms. Vance said the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions. "We're not going to trade words for actions," Vance said.  UNCLEAR HOW IRAN MAKES DECISIONS: VANCE Complicating matters, Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran. Vance said the US was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran's power structure, he said, after joint US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.  "One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his "biggest problem" is no one knows who is running Iran.  Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that US officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran's decision-making system works. "The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials," Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference.

Related:

Commentary: Who in Iran can make a deal with the US – and make it stick?

White House denies Trump suggested Iran should 'take out' US cities

Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions. He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway. The war - and its US$3 billion monthly price tag - has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.  Vance has sought to temper criticism of Trump’s handling of the conflict, telling voters they should not let that issue keep them from backing Republicans in next month's elections. In Alaska, Vance rallied for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight reelection battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Trump carried Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but rising everyday costs have put the state in play. Before speaking with Reuters, Vance focused much of his speech on affordability concerns, especially around energy. Alaska's remote locale makes consumer goods more expensive, and energy production is a key industry. Rally attendees roared when Sullivan nearly introduced Vance as the president of the US, rather than the vice president. Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House.  Vance told Reuters afterward that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028. "I'm inherently a procrastinator," he said. "I really haven't thought about it much."
